---
title: "Practical work: prepare, record, evaluate"
---

These materials support preparation and interpretation. Perform laboratory
work only with your department's approved protocol, supervision and local
safety instructions. Your instructor will supply the actual experimental
arrangements. The provided CSVs are constructed teaching data.

## Keep primary records

Record date, sample identifiers, reagent amounts, relevant conditions,
observations and deviations in your laboratory journal as the work happens.
Retain instrument files and photographs with their sample labels. An Rmd report
draws on those records; it does not replace the original observations.

## Before a reaction: calculate the amount table

For the teaching equation salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + ethanoic
acid, all coefficients are one. With 1.3812 g salicylic acid (138.12 g/mol)
and 1.53135 g acetic anhydride (102.09 g/mol), the amounts are 10.0 and 15.0 mmol.
The acid limits the theoretical aspirin amount to 10.0 mmol. The reaction
scheme is a calculation context, not an operating protocol.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
amounts
```

Compare amount divided by coefficient rather than mass alone. In a different
balanced reaction, a coefficient of two would change that comparison.

## TLC: retain every spot

For the supplied normal-phase teaching plate, the solvent front travels 5.0 cm
from the origin. A starting-material spot travels 1.2 cm and a product spot
3.2 cm. Their Rf values are 0.24 and 0.64. The crude lane contains both spots.

```r
tlc <- read_csv("data/tlc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Rf = spot_distance_cm / front_distance_cm)
tlc
```

Explain why the crude has two rows. Do not average two different spots into
one fictitious compound. Compare Rf only under matched conditions. Co-migration
does not prove identity, and a single visible spot does not prove purity.

## After isolation: distinguish the claims

With product molar mass 180.16 g/mol, theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. An isolated
mass of 1.20 g corresponds to 66.6% isolated yield.

```r
theoretical_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
```

Yield is not conversion. Loss during work-up can lower isolated yield even
after substantial reaction. Residual solvent or impurities can inflate mass.
Assess identity and purity using appropriate evidence and uncertainty.

## A compact report structure

Use the [starter Rmd](../templates/report.Rmd), preferably through the complete
[project download](../downloads/organic-chemistry-student.zip).

1. State the chemical question and include a checked reaction drawing.
2. Identify the protocol and primary records; distinguish performed work from teaching data.
3. Show the amount table with units and limiting-reagent reasoning.
4. Present observations, spectra and TLC with sample labels and captions.
5. Calculate yield from saved data and connect conclusions to evidence.
6. Discuss limitations and alternative explanations.
7. Restart R and Knit from the saved project before submitting source, data and output as instructed.

The example IR traces in the starter compare ethanol and ethyl ethanoate.
They are **not measurements of the aspirin isolation**. Keep that distinction
in your report rather than combining unrelated samples into one claim.
